why_how.text: The handbook's first rule in any emergency is not to panic but to react quickly and correctly.
Brake failure has a set response that differs between manual and automatic cars.

scenario.text: Sam is driving an automatic car downhill when the brake pedal stops working.

reasoning.text: If the brakes fail in an automatic car, apply the emergency brake and move the gear lever into the low range.

result.text: Sam applies the emergency brake and selects low range, accepting possible damage because there is no better option.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the manual-car brake failure steps in an automatic.

correction.text: A manual car downshifts and releases the clutch before the emergency brake, while an automatic applies the emergency brake and selects low range.

prompt.text: Sam's brakes fail in an automatic car. What two steps does the handbook give?

answer.text: Apply the emergency brake and move the gear lever into low range.

rationale.text: The automatic response is the emergency brake plus low range, while a manual first downshifts and releases the clutch.

narration.text: This chapter covers emergencies and crashes: what to do when equipment fails, when tires blow out, when you leave the road or start to skid, when a crash is coming, and what the law requires afterward. This first lesson covers three topics. First, what to do after you hit an animal or find an injured one. Second, the handbook's first rule for any emergency. Third, how to respond when the brakes fail, which the handbook describes differently for manual and automatic cars. Practice questions often test that manual and automatic difference.

lines.text: Stay in the car, doors locked.
Hazard lights on; do not approach.

narration.text: After hitting an animal or finding an injured one, pull safely to the roadside, stay in the car with the doors locked and turn on the hazard lights. Do not walk up to an animal you have struck, because it may be dangerous. So the handbook's steps keep you protected inside the car, off the travel lanes, with your hazard lights warning other drivers. Approaching the animal is the one step it specifically rules out. The handbook also lists reporting contacts for animal collisions, which you can look up in the current handbook when needed.

lines.text: Manual: lower gear, clutch, emergency brake.
Automatic: emergency brake and low range.

narration.text: In any emergency, the first rule is not to panic but to react quickly and correctly. If the brakes fail in a manual car, shift to a lower gear, release the clutch and apply the emergency brake. If the brakes fail in an automatic car, apply the emergency brake and move the gear lever into the low range. Using the emergency brake and low gear this way may damage them, but with failed brakes there is no better option. So the handbook accepts possible damage to the emergency brake and transmission in exchange for slowing a car whose brakes have failed.

lines.text: Manual: downshift and release the clutch first.
Automatic: emergency brake and low range.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The two brake-failure responses use some of the same tools but in a different order. With failed brakes, a manual car downshifts and releases the clutch before the emergency brake, while an automatic applies the emergency brake and selects low range. Practice questions may describe an automatic and offer releasing the clutch, or describe a manual and leave out the downshift. Identify the transmission first, then match the steps. Both responses end with the car being slowed by the emergency brake and a low gear, as the handbook describes.

lines.text: Emergency brake and low gear may be damaged.

narration.text: Some drivers hesitate to use the emergency brake or a low gear at speed, worried about damaging the car. The handbook addresses that directly. Using the emergency brake and low gear this way may damage them, but with failed brakes there is no better option. This connects back to the first rule of any emergency: do not panic, and react quickly and correctly. So if the brakes fail, the handbook's guidance is to act at once with the emergency brake and a low gear, using the order that matches your car, rather than waiting or worrying about repair costs.

Here is a quick check: Sam is driving an automatic car down a long hill when the brake pedal suddenly stops working. Sam remembers not to panic. What two steps does the handbook give for this situation? Work it out before reading on. Sam should apply the emergency brake and move the gear lever into the low range. That is the automatic response. A manual car would instead shift to a lower gear, release the clutch and then apply the emergency brake. The handbook notes that these steps may cause damage, but with failed brakes there is no better option.

lines.text: Pull over, stay inside, hazards on.
Manual downshifts first; automatic uses low range.

narration.text: Let us recap. After hitting an animal or finding an injured one, pull safely to the roadside, stay in the car with the doors locked and turn on the hazard lights, and do not walk up to the animal. In any emergency, do not panic; react quickly and correctly. If the brakes fail in a manual car, shift to a lower gear, release the clutch and apply the emergency brake. In an automatic, apply the emergency brake and move the gear lever into low range. These steps may damage the car, but with failed brakes there is no better option.

why_how.text: The handbook gives different brake techniques for wet brakes and long downhills.
A stuck gas pedal has its own response, different from brake failure.

scenario.text: Pat's gas pedal sticks while driving on a highway.

reasoning.text: If the gas pedal sticks, tap or lift it with your foot, shift to neutral and brake firmly without locking the wheels, then get completely off the road.

result.text: Pat shifts to neutral, brakes firmly without locking the wheels, and pulls completely off the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a stuck gas pedal like brake failure and reaching for the emergency brake and a low gear.

correction.text: A stuck gas pedal calls for shifting to neutral and braking firmly, whereas brake failure calls for a lower gear and the emergency brake.

prompt.text: Pat's gas pedal sticks on the highway. Should Pat shift to neutral or to a lower gear?

answer.text: Neutral, then brake firmly without locking the wheels.

rationale.text: A stuck gas pedal calls for neutral and firm braking, while brake failure calls for a lower gear and the emergency brake.

narration.text: This lesson covers three more brake and pedal situations. First, what to do when the brakes are wet, for example after driving through deep water. Second, how to control speed on a long or steep downhill. Third, how to respond when the gas pedal sticks. The handbook gives a different technique for each, and two of them involve the brake pedal in opposite ways: one uses light braking on purpose, and the other spares the brake pedal and uses the engine instead. The stuck-pedal response is also easy to confuse with the brake-failure response from the last lesson.

lines.text: Wet brakes: short drive, light pressure.
Long downhill: lower gear, not the pedal.

narration.text: To dry wet brakes, drive a short distance while pressing lightly on the brake pedal, so the friction heat evaporates the water. On a long or steep downhill, control speed with a lower gear rather than the brake pedal, shifting down at the top before you start down. So these two situations call for opposite uses of the pedal. With wet brakes, you use the pedal lightly on purpose to warm and dry them. On a long downhill, you spare the pedal and let a lower gear hold the speed, choosing that gear before the descent begins.

lines.text: Tap or lift the pedal with your foot.
Do not lock the wheels; get off the road.

narration.text: If the gas pedal sticks, tap it or lift it with your foot, shift to neutral and brake firmly without locking the wheels, then get completely off the road. So the handbook's response has four steps. Try to free the pedal with your foot, take the engine out of gear by shifting to neutral, brake firmly but not so hard that the wheels lock, and then leave the road entirely. Once the engine is in neutral, the stuck pedal no longer pushes the car forward, so the brakes can bring it to a stop and you can get safely off the road.

lines.text: Stuck gas pedal: neutral and firm braking.
Failed brakes: lower gear and emergency brake.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A stuck gas pedal calls for shifting to neutral and braking firmly, whereas brake failure calls for a lower gear and the emergency brake. The two emergencies feel similar because the car will not slow the way you want, but the handbook's responses differ. Practice questions may describe a stuck gas pedal and offer the emergency brake and low gear, or describe failed brakes and offer neutral. Ask which part has failed. If the brakes do not work, use a lower gear and the emergency brake. If the gas pedal is stuck, shift to neutral and brake firmly.

Here is a quick check: Pat is driving on a highway when the gas pedal sticks and the car keeps speeding up. Should Pat shift to neutral or to a lower gear? Work it out before reading on. Pat should shift to neutral. If the gas pedal sticks, tap it or lift it with your foot, shift to neutral and brake firmly without locking the wheels, then get completely off the road. A lower gear and the emergency brake belong to a different emergency, brake failure. Here the brakes still work, so neutral and firm braking bring the car to a stop.

lines.text: Downhill: gear down at the top.

narration.text: To finish, dry wet brakes by driving a short distance while pressing lightly on the brake pedal. On a long or steep downhill, control speed with a lower gear rather than the brake pedal, shifting down at the top. If the gas pedal sticks, tap or lift it with your foot, shift to neutral, brake firmly without locking the wheels and get completely off the road. Keep the stuck-pedal response separate from brake failure, which calls for a lower gear and the emergency brake. Next, tire problems and blowouts. Neutral and firm braking, then off the road.

why_how.text: The handbook says a blowout comes with a loud noise and a swerve, and gives a set response to keep control.
Changing a flat or making repairs has its own safety steps, starting with getting fully off the road.

scenario.text: Lee hears a loud bang and the car swerves on the highway.

reasoning.text: In a blowout, grip the wheel firmly and keep the car straight in your lane, then slow down by lifting off the accelerator, and do not brake until the engine has slowed the car.

result.text: Lee holds the car straight, lifts off the gas, brakes only after the car has slowed, and pulls completely off the road.

claim.text: Common mistake: braking hard the moment a tire blows out.

correction.text: During a blowout you hold the wheel straight and avoid braking until the engine slows the car, while a flat tire change starts only once the car is fully off the road.

prompt.text: Lee's tire blows out with a loud bang. When should Lee brake?

answer.text: Only after the engine has slowed the car enough to keep control.

rationale.text: The handbook says hold the car straight, lift off the gas, and wait to brake until the car has slowed.

narration.text: This lesson covers tire problems. You will review the warning signs that something is wrong with a tire, how a blowout announces itself, the steps for keeping control during a blowout, when to brake afterward, and the safety steps for changing a flat: where to stop, what to set, where passengers wait, which lights to use, how to keep the car from rolling, and when not to attempt a repair at all. The blowout response is the part practice questions test most, because the handbook tells you to do something that runs against instinct.

lines.text: Bumpy ride: stop and check tires.
Blowout: loud noise and a swerve.
Grip, keep straight, lift off the gas.

narration.text: An unexplained bumpy ride is a reason to stop and check the tires. A blowout announces itself with a loud noise and a swerve. In a blowout, grip the wheel firmly and keep the car straight in your lane, then slow down by lifting off the accelerator. So the handbook separates an early warning from the emergency itself. A bumpy ride with no clear cause means stop and look. A loud bang and a swerve mean a blowout, and your hands and feet each have a job: hands grip the wheel and hold the car straight, and your foot comes off the gas.

title.text: When to brake after a blowout

lines.text: Let the engine slow the car.
Then pull completely off the road.

narration.text: After a blowout, do not brake until the engine has slowed the car enough for you to keep control, then pull completely off the road. So braking comes late in the blowout response, not first. You hold the car straight and lift off the gas, and the engine begins to slow the car. Only once the speed has come down enough that you can keep control do you brake, and then you move all the way off the road. The handbook's order is grip, straight, lift off, wait, then brake and pull off, with no sudden moves in between. Grip, straight, lift off, then brake.

lines.text: Brake only after the car slows.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a tire blows, the instinct is to brake hard. The handbook says otherwise. During a blowout you hold the wheel straight and avoid braking until the engine slows the car, while a flat tire change starts only once the car is fully off the road. Practice questions may offer braking hard, or steering sharply onto the shoulder, as the first response. Neither matches the handbook. The first response is to grip the wheel, keep the car straight and lift off the gas. Braking and pulling off come after the car has slowed.

lines.text: Fully off the road, parking brake set.
Flares out if you have them.

narration.text: Before changing a flat, move fully off the road, set the parking brake and put out flares if you have them. During a tire change, all passengers must get out on the passenger side and wait off the road, never standing in front of or behind the car. So the handbook's tire-change steps start with location and position. The car must be fully off the road with the parking brake set, flares out if available, and every passenger out of the car on the side away from traffic, waiting off the road and not in front of or behind the car.

lines.text: Never repair beside traffic; call for help.

narration.text: Turn on the flashers and parking lights and block the wheels so the car cannot roll while the tire is changed. Never try to repair a car where it is exposed to passing traffic; call a tow truck or mechanic instead. So once the car is off the road, the handbook adds lights to warn other drivers and blocks to keep the car from rolling. And it draws a firm line: if the car is somewhere exposed to passing traffic, do not attempt the repair at all. Call a tow truck or a mechanic and wait safely away from the road. A tow truck is the safe choice there.

lines.text: A loud bang on the highway.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lee is driving on the highway when there is a loud bang and the car swerves. Lee grips the wheel firmly and keeps the car straight in the lane. When should Lee brake? Work it out before reading on. Only after the engine has slowed the car enough for Lee to keep control. In a blowout, grip the wheel, keep the car straight and lift off the accelerator, and do not brake until the car has slowed. Then Lee pulls completely off the road and, once fully off, can set the parking brake and begin a safe tire change.

lines.text: Blowout: grip, straight, lift off, brake later.
Change flats fully off the road.

narration.text: Let us recap. An unexplained bumpy ride is a reason to stop and check the tires, and a blowout comes with a loud noise and a swerve. In a blowout, grip the wheel, keep the car straight and lift off the accelerator, and do not brake until the engine has slowed the car; then pull completely off the road. To change a flat, move fully off the road, set the parking brake, put out flares, have passengers exit on the passenger side and wait off the road, use the flashers and parking lights, and block the wheels. Never repair a car beside passing traffic.

why_how.text: The handbook says to get the car fully onto the shoulder and everyone out on the passenger side, standing well away.
A white cloth and a raised hood signal for help, and a flashlight or flares should always be in the car.

scenario.text: Morgan's car breaks down on a highway in the evening.

reasoning.text: Move the car fully onto the shoulder, get everyone out on the passenger side, tie a white cloth to the left door handle or aerial, raise the hood, and after dark use the parking lights or flashers.

result.text: Morgan and the passengers wait well away from the car, not in front of it or behind it.

claim.text: Common mistake: waiting inside or behind a broken-down car on the shoulder.

correction.text: Everyone should get out on the passenger side and stand well away from the car, not in front of it or behind it.

prompt.text: Morgan's car breaks down on the highway at dusk. How does Morgan signal for help?

answer.text: A white cloth on the left door handle or aerial, the hood raised, and parking lights or flashers after dark.

rationale.text: The handbook's help signal is the white cloth and raised hood, with everyone out on the passenger side.

lines.text: Get off the road and out.

narration.text: This lesson covers what to do when your car breaks down. The handbook gives three groups of steps. First, where to put the car and where the people in it should be. Second, how to signal that you need help, both in daylight and after dark. Third, what to keep in the car at all times so that you are ready for an emergency. These steps connect to the tire-change rules from the last lesson, which also had passengers exit on the passenger side and wait away from the car. Practice questions often test where people should stand and what the help signal looks like.

lines.text: Stand well away, not in front or behind.

narration.text: In a breakdown, move the car fully onto the shoulder, get everyone out on the passenger side and stand well away from the car, not in front of it or behind it. So the handbook's first priority is distance from traffic. The car goes all the way onto the shoulder. The people get out on the side away from the travel lanes. And they stand well away from the car, specifically not in front of it or behind it, where they would be in line with the vehicle. This is the same pattern the handbook uses for passengers during a tire change.

lines.text: White cloth on the left door handle or aerial.
After dark: parking lights or flashers.

narration.text: To ask for help after a breakdown, tie a white cloth to the left door handle or the radio aerial and raise the hood. After dark, use the parking lights or flashers. Keep a flashlight or flares in the car at all times for emergencies. So the handbook's help signal has two parts that work in daylight, the white cloth and the raised hood, and adds lights after dark. A flashlight or flares, kept in the car all the time, make it possible to see and be seen when a breakdown happens at night or in poor weather. Keep a flashlight or flares in the car.

lines.text: White cloth: left door handle or aerial.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A breakdown signal for help is a white cloth on the left door handle or aerial plus a raised hood, and everyone exits on the passenger side. Practice questions may offer a raised trunk, a cloth on the right side mirror, or exiting on the driver's side. None of these match the handbook. The cloth goes on the left door handle or the radio aerial, the hood goes up, and people get out on the passenger side, away from traffic. After dark, the parking lights or flashers are added. Keep each detail exact.

Here is a quick check: Morgan's car breaks down on a highway at dusk. Morgan has moved the car fully onto the shoulder and everyone has gotten out on the passenger side. How should Morgan signal for help? Work it out before reading on. Morgan should tie a white cloth to the left door handle or the radio aerial and raise the hood, and because it is getting dark, turn on the parking lights or flashers. Morgan and the passengers then wait well away from the car, not in front of it or behind it, with a flashlight or flares ready.

lines.text: Shoulder, out the passenger side, stand away.
Lights after dark; flashlight or flares.

narration.text: To finish, in a breakdown, move the car fully onto the shoulder, get everyone out on the passenger side and stand well away from the car, not in front of it or behind it. To ask for help, tie a white cloth to the left door handle or radio aerial and raise the hood, and after dark use the parking lights or flashers. Keep a flashlight or flares in the car at all times for emergencies. These steps keep people away from passing traffic while letting other drivers and officers see that you need help. Stand well away from the car.

why_how.text: The handbook says to slow, sound the horn and keep right when an oncoming car crosses into your lane, even if that means leaving the road.
If your wheels drop onto the shoulder, the handbook warns against hard braking or jerking back, because you could skid or roll over.

scenario.text: Taylor's right wheels drift off the pavement onto a soft shoulder.

reasoning.text: Do not brake hard or jerk back; ease off the gas, steer straight, let the engine slow the car, and return gradually once traffic is clear and you are nearly stopped.

result.text: Taylor eases off, holds the car straight, slows almost to a stop, and returns to the pavement when the lane is clear.

claim.text: Common mistake: jerking the wheel back toward the road as soon as the wheels leave the pavement.

correction.text: Running onto the shoulder means no hard braking and no sharp turn back, while an oncoming car in your lane means keep right even off the road.

prompt.text: Taylor's right wheels drop off the pavement. Should Taylor jerk the wheel back right away?

answer.text: No; ease off the gas, steer straight, slow down and return gradually.

rationale.text: Jerking back or braking hard could cause a skid or rollover, so the handbook calls for a slow, gradual return.

lines.text: An oncoming car in your lane.

narration.text: This lesson covers two situations where your car may end up off the pavement. The first is an oncoming vehicle crossing the center line into your path, where the handbook tells you to keep right even if it means leaving the road. The second is when your wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder by accident, where the handbook tells you to avoid sudden moves and return gradually. These two call for different responses, and practice questions often place them side by side, so learn what makes each one different.

lines.text: Keep right, even off the road.

narration.text: If an oncoming vehicle crosses the center line into your path, slow down at once and sound the horn. When a vehicle crosses into your lane, keep to the right, even if that means leaving the road. So the handbook's response to a head-on threat is to reduce speed, warn the other driver with the horn, and move right, away from the oncoming vehicle. Going off the road to the right is preferred over staying in its path. Moving left, into the lane the other driver has left, is not what the handbook describes. Keep right and slow down.

lines.text: Do not jerk back toward the road.
Ease off, steer straight, let the engine slow you.

narration.text: If your wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder, do not brake hard or jerk back toward the road, since you could skid or roll over. To recover from running onto the shoulder, ease off the gas, steer straight, let the engine slow the car, and return gradually only once traffic is clear and you are nearly stopped. So the recovery is slow and deliberate. Hold the car straight on the shoulder, let it lose speed, and only when you are nearly stopped and the lane is clear do you ease back onto the pavement. Return only when nearly stopped.

lines.text: Shoulder drop: no hard brakes, no sharp turn.
Oncoming car: keep right, even off the road.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Running onto the shoulder means no hard braking and no sharp turn back, while an oncoming car in your lane means keep right even off the road. Practice questions may describe wheels dropping off the pavement and offer a quick jerk back onto the road, or describe an oncoming car and offer swerving left. Neither matches the handbook. Identify the situation first. If your own wheels slipped off the edge, recover gently and gradually. If an oncoming car is in your lane, slow, sound the horn and keep right.

Here is a quick check: Taylor is driving on a two-lane road when the right wheels drift off the pavement onto a soft shoulder. Should Taylor jerk the wheel back toward the road right away? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Do not brake hard or jerk back toward the road, since you could skid or roll over. Taylor should ease off the gas, steer straight, let the engine slow the car, and return gradually only once traffic is clear and the car is nearly stopped. The quick jerk back is the move the handbook warns against.

lines.text: Oncoming car: slow, horn, keep right.
Shoulder drop: no hard brakes or jerks.

narration.text: To finish, if an oncoming vehicle crosses the center line into your path, slow down at once, sound the horn and keep to the right, even if that means leaving the road. If your wheels drop off the pavement onto the shoulder, do not brake hard or jerk back toward the road, since you could skid or roll over. Instead, ease off the gas, steer straight, let the engine slow the car, and return gradually only once traffic is clear and you are nearly stopped. Keep the two situations and their responses separate. Return gradually once the lane is clear.

why_how.text: The handbook says wet roads, ice and packed snow make skids more likely, so reduce speed gradually on them.
Braking to avoid a skid differs with and without ABS, and correcting a skid takes two steering moves in order.

scenario.text: On an icy curve, the rear of Kai's car begins to slide to the right.

reasoning.text: In a skid, ease off the gas and steer toward the direction the rear of the car is sliding, then turn back as the car straightens.

result.text: Kai eases off the gas, steers right toward the slide, then turns back as the car straightens so it does not over-steer.

claim.text: Common mistake: steering away from the direction the rear of the car is sliding.

correction.text: In a skid you first steer toward the rear's slide and then steer back as the car straightens, so the two steering moves happen in sequence.

prompt.text: The rear of Kai's car slides to the right on ice. Which way should Kai steer first?

answer.text: To the right, toward the slide, after easing off the gas.

rationale.text: Steer toward the direction the rear is sliding, then turn back as the car straightens.

narration.text: This lesson covers skids. You will review which road surfaces make skids more likely, how to brake to avoid a skid in a car with anti-lock brakes and in a car without them, and how to steer once a skid has started. Correcting a skid takes two steering moves in a specific order, and practice questions often test that order. The braking methods also differ sharply depending on whether the car has ABS, so as you study, keep the ABS method and the non-ABS method in separate boxes. Prevention starts with slowing gradually on wet roads, ice and packed snow.

lines.text: Wet, ice and packed snow raise skid risk.
ABS: firm, steady. No ABS: pump gently.

narration.text: Wet roads, ice and packed snow make skids more likely, so reduce speed gradually on them. To avoid a skid with ABS, press the brake firmly and steadily without pumping. Without ABS, pump the brakes gently. So prevention starts with speed. On slippery surfaces, slow down gradually rather than suddenly. If you need to brake hard, the method depends on the car. With anti-lock brakes, hold firm, steady pressure. Without them, pump the brakes gently. The handbook gives these as two different methods for two kinds of brakes.

Here is a trap about braking. With ABS you hold firm steady pressure to avoid a skid, but without ABS you pump the brakes gently. Practice questions may reverse these, offering pumping for an ABS car or steady pressure for a car without ABS. Check the car first. If the question says the car has anti-lock brakes, the answer is firm, steady pressure, never pumping. If it says the car has no ABS, the answer is to pump gently. This matches the ABS advice in the equipment chapter, where pumping was said to reduce how well ABS works.

In a skid, ease off the gas and steer toward the direction the rear of the car is sliding. As the car begins to straighten out of the skid, turn the wheel back the other way so you do not over-steer. So the correction has two moves. First, steer in the same direction the rear of the car is sliding. Second, as the car starts to come back into line, turn the wheel back so you do not swing too far the other way. Your foot comes off the gas at the start, and the steering does the work. Steer toward the slide, then turn back as it straightens.

Here is the second trap. In a skid you first steer toward the rear's slide and then steer back as the car straightens, so the two steering moves happen in sequence. Practice questions may describe only the first move, or reverse the order, or suggest steering away from the slide. None of these match the handbook. If the rear of the car slides right, steer right. Then, as the car straightens, turn back to avoid over-steering. The memory line captures the first and most important move: steer where the rear slides. Steer where the rear slides.

Here is a quick check: Kai is driving around an icy curve when the rear of the car begins to slide to the right. Which way should Kai steer first? Work it out before reading on. Kai should ease off the gas and steer to the right, toward the direction the rear of the car is sliding. Then, as the car begins to straighten out, Kai turns the wheel back the other way so the car does not over-steer. If Kai needs to brake on that ice, the method depends on the car: firm, steady pressure with ABS, or gentle pumping without it.

To finish, wet roads, ice and packed snow make skids more likely, so reduce speed gradually on them. To avoid a skid with ABS, press the brake firmly and steadily without pumping; without ABS, pump the brakes gently. In a skid, ease off the gas and steer toward the direction the rear of the car is sliding, and as the car begins to straighten, turn the wheel back so you do not over-steer. Those two steering moves happen in order. Next, what to do in the moments before a crash. Hold with ABS, pump without it, and steer toward the slide.

why_how.text: The handbook gives last-moment actions for oncoming and rear threats to reduce harm.
North Carolina law protects people who stop to help at a crash from civil liability, with exceptions.

scenario.text: Riley sees in the mirror that a car behind is about to hit Riley's car, and the road ahead is clear.

reasoning.text: With clear road ahead, accelerate away, be ready to brake if space runs out, brace yourself and press your head against the head rest.

result.text: Riley accelerates away, stays ready to brake, and braces with the head pressed against the head rest.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should brake hard when a rear impact is coming and the road ahead is clear.

correction.text: If a rear impact is coming and the road ahead is clear, accelerate away, but also brace and press your head against the head rest.

prompt.text: A car is about to hit Riley from behind, and the road ahead is clear. What should Riley do?

answer.text: Accelerate away, be ready to brake, brace and press the head against the head rest.

rationale.text: The handbook pairs accelerating away with bracing when a rear impact is coming and the road ahead is open.

narration.text: This lesson covers the moments just before a crash and one legal point about helping afterward. You will review what to do when a crash with oncoming traffic seems likely, what to do when you are about to be struck from behind, how to hold the wheel and protect yourself at the moment of impact, and the North Carolina law that protects people who stop to help at a crash. The handbook's advice here is specific, and practice questions usually describe a threat from one direction and ask for the matching response. Each threat has its own response.

lines.text: Head-on: horn, keep right, turn away.
Brace, head against the head rest.

narration.text: If a crash seems likely, sound the horn, keep right and turn away from oncoming traffic, even into an open field off the road. If you are about to be struck from behind with clear road ahead, accelerate away, be ready to brake if space runs out, brace yourself and press your head against the head rest. So the handbook's response depends on where the threat comes from. From the front, warn, keep right and turn away, even off the road. From behind, with space ahead, move forward, stay ready to brake, and brace with your head back against the rest.

lines.text: Rear impact, clear road: accelerate away.
Also brace, head against the head rest.

narration.text: Here is the trap. If a rear impact is coming and the road ahead is clear, you accelerate away, but you also brace and press your head against the head rest. Practice questions may offer braking hard, or leaning forward, as the response to a coming rear impact. Neither matches the handbook. When there is clear road ahead, moving forward can reduce the impact, and pressing your head against the head rest is part of bracing. And be ready to brake if the space ahead runs out. Memory line: speed away, then brace. Be ready to brake if space runs out.

lines.text: Be ready to turn to control the car.

narration.text: If you are about to be hit, hold the steering wheel tightly. If a crash is about to happen, be ready to turn quickly to try to control the car, and as a last resort shield your face from breaking glass with your arms and hands. So in the final moment, the handbook's priorities are keeping control and then protecting yourself. A tight grip on the wheel and readiness to steer help you control the car. Only as a last resort does the handbook suggest using your arms and hands to shield your face from glass. Hold the wheel tightly.

lines.text: Helping at a crash is protected.
Except intentional wrongdoing or unruly conduct.

narration.text: North Carolina law shields people who stop to help at a crash from civil liability, except for intentional wrongdoing or unruly conduct. So the handbook reassures drivers who stop to help that the law protects them from civil lawsuits for helping, with two exceptions. Intentional wrongdoing is not protected, and neither is unruly conduct. The next lesson covers the duties every driver involved in a crash has, including helping the injured and making sure law enforcement is notified, which this protection is meant to support.

lines.text: A car is about to hit from behind.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Riley glances in the mirror and sees that the car behind is not slowing and is about to hit Riley's car. The road ahead is clear. What should Riley do? Work it out before reading on. Riley should accelerate away, be ready to brake if the space ahead runs out, brace, and press the head against the head rest. If the threat were an oncoming car instead, the handbook's response would be to sound the horn, keep right and turn away, even into an open field off the road. Either way, Riley holds the wheel tightly.

lines.text: Head-on: horn, keep right, turn away.
Hold the wheel; shield your face last.

narration.text: Let us recap. If a crash seems likely, sound the horn, keep right and turn away from oncoming traffic, even into an open field off the road. If you are about to be struck from behind with clear road ahead, accelerate away, be ready to brake if space runs out, brace yourself and press your head against the head rest. If you are about to be hit, hold the steering wheel tightly, be ready to turn quickly to control the car, and as a last resort shield your face from breaking glass. North Carolina law shields people who stop to help at a crash from civil liability, except for intentional wrongdoing or unruly conduct.

why_how.text: Every driver involved in a crash must stop, and the handbook lists duties at the scene.
Reporting rules depend on injuries and the amount of damage, and failing to report has penalties.

scenario.text: Jamie is in a crash on a highway lane with no injuries, but the damage to both cars looks well over one thousand dollars.

reasoning.text: With no injuries, drivable cars move out of the travel lane onto the shoulder, and apparent damage of one thousand dollars or more must be reported to law enforcement right away.

result.text: Jamie moves the car to the shoulder, reports the crash to the nearest officer, exchanges information, and also tells the insurance company.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking only crashes with injuries need to be reported to police.

correction.text: A crash must be reported to police right away for any death or injury, or for apparent damage of one thousand dollars or more, while reporting to your insurer is advised for every crash.

prompt.text: Jamie's crash injured no one, but damage looks well over one thousand dollars. Must Jamie report it to law enforcement?

rationale.text: Apparent damage of one thousand dollars or more triggers the police report even without injuries.

narration.text: This last lesson in the chapter covers what you must do after a crash. You will review the duty to stop, what to do at the scene, when drivable cars should be moved out of the travel lane, when a crash must be reported to law enforcement, the penalties for not reporting, reporting to your insurer and DMV forms, the information you must exchange, and what to do when you cannot identify the other people or the owner of damaged property. The reporting threshold is the most tested point, so pay special attention to it.

lines.text: Prevent further crashes, help the injured.

narration.text: A driver involved in a crash must stop immediately; failing to stop breaks the law. At a crash scene, take steps to prevent further crashes, help the injured and make sure someone notifies law enforcement right away. If nobody is hurt or killed in a crash on a highway lane, ramp or shoulder, each car that can be driven safely should be moved out of the travel lane onto the shoulder. So the scene duties are to stop, protect against more crashes, help anyone hurt, get police notified, and, when no one is hurt, clear drivable cars out of the travel lane.

lines.text: Or damage of one thousand dollars or more.

narration.text: You must report a crash to the nearest law enforcement officer or agency right away if anyone is killed or injured, or if total property damage appears to be one thousand dollars or more. Not reporting a reportable crash can lead to prosecution and suspension of your driver license. So two kinds of crashes must be reported: those with any death or injury, and those where the damage appears to reach one thousand dollars or more, even with no one hurt. The penalty for skipping a required report includes possible prosecution and loss of your license.

lines.text: Police: death, injury, or one thousand dollars.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A crash must be reported to police right away for any death or injury, or for apparent damage of one thousand dollars or more, while reporting to your insurer is advised for every crash. Practice questions may suggest that only injury crashes go to police, or that insurers need to hear only about serious crashes. Neither matches the handbook. Police reporting has the injury and damage threshold. Insurer reporting has no threshold. And in some cases you must also file DMV forms proving liability insurance.

lines.text: Report every crash to your insurer.
Some cases need DMV insurance forms.
Exchange name, address, license, registration, insurer.

narration.text: You should also report any crash to your insurance company, and in some cases you must file DMV forms proving liability insurance. After a crash you must give your name, address, license number, vehicle registration number and insurance company, and collect the same from the others involved. If you cannot identify the other occupants or the owner of damaged property, write down everything you can and give it to the nearest law enforcement officer. So the information exchange goes both ways, and when it cannot happen, the information goes to law enforcement instead.

lines.text: Damage looks over one thousand dollars.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jamie is in a crash on a highway. No one is hurt, but the damage to both cars appears to be well over one thousand dollars. Must Jamie report the crash to law enforcement? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes, right away. A crash must be reported to the nearest law enforcement officer or agency if anyone is killed or injured, or if total property damage appears to be one thousand dollars or more. Jamie also moves the drivable car onto the shoulder, exchanges information, and reports the crash to the insurance company.

lines.text: Always stop; help and notify police.
Report injuries or a thousand dollars of damage.

narration.text: To finish the chapter, a driver involved in a crash must stop immediately. Prevent further crashes, help the injured and make sure law enforcement is notified, and if no one is hurt, move drivable cars out of the travel lane onto the shoulder. Report the crash to law enforcement right away if anyone is killed or injured or damage appears to be one thousand dollars or more; failing to report can mean prosecution and suspension. Report every crash to your insurer, exchange names, addresses, license and registration numbers and insurers, and give what you can to police if others cannot be identified.
